 STAFF REPORT

  COMMUNITY
  DEVELOPMENT

DATE:  August 26, 2026

TO:  Transportation Commission

FROM:  David Kriske, Assistant Community Development Director, Transportation
  BY: Chris Buonomo, Senior Transportation Planner

SUBJECT: Discussion of the Draft Downtown Transit Oriented Development Specific
  Plan

RECOMMENDATION
Receive an update on the Draft Downtown Transit Oriented Development Specific Plan.

BACKGROUND
The Downtown Burbank Transit Oriented Development Specific Plan (Downtown TOD
Specific Plan or Specific Plan) is a new specific plan that provides policy direction for the
future land development and public improvements of the 918-acre Plan Area located
within the central portion of the City of Burbank (City). The Specific Plan replaces two
existing planning documents, the 1997 Burbank Center Plan and the 2012 North San
Fernando Boulevard Master Plan. The new plan builds on these prior planning efforts and
establishes a coordinated policy framework, unified land use vision, and objective
development standards to guide future growth and reinvestment in Downtown Burbank
(Downtown).

The Specific Plan is intended to address the demand for workforce and affordable
housing by facilitating the infill development of housing opportunity sites, update zoning
regulations to incentive public and private investment in housing, create new
placemaking opportunities that include redevelopment of the Burbank Town Center and
City Civic Center areas, and create complete streets with improved connectivity through
a unified vision for Downtown Burbank.
 Development of the Downtown TOD Specific Plan is funded through the following
sources:
  • Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transit Authority (METRO) – Transit Oriented
  Development Planning Grant Program
  • California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) – SB 2
  Planning Grant Program
  • City General Funds (previously authorized by City Council)

DISCUSSION
While much of the Downtown TOD Plan focuses on land use and housing; transportation
policies, objectives, and projects are vital pieces of the future vision for Downtown. With
an increase in residential use and a balancing of commercial opportunities across
Downtown, the plan identifies the need to move new residents and visitors effectively
within existing roadway constraints and possible new future transportation connections.
The following chapters specifically address the future transportation system for Downtown
Burbank: Public Realm (Chapter 5), Circulation and Mobility (Chapter 6), and Parking
(Chapter 7).

Public Realm (Chapter 5)
Objectives for the public realm in Downtown focus on tree cover, greenery, open space,
and wayfinding as a way to improve the visual identity of the area and enhance the user
experience of its streets. Proposed strategies include expanding the urban forest and
drought tolerant plantings, as well as introducing various types of publicly accessible open
spaces, including the activation and enhancement of existing alleys and paseos, to
promote vibrant Downtown street life. These strategies can be implemented in the new
Civic Center, along the re-aligned San Fernando Boulevard, and on existing parkways
and alleys.

Circulation and Mobility (Chapter 6)
The Circulation and Mobility chapter outlines multimodal objectives that align with and
build upon those established in previous transportation planning documents, including the
Complete Streets Plan, Bicycle Master Plan, and the Burbank2035 General Plan Mobility
Element. Strategies include providing safer and more appealing access to transit; building
a multimodal, pedestrian friendly environment within existing network; expanding non-
vehicular access as part of new infill development; and strengthening first/last mile
connections between the Metrolink Station and amenities in Downtown.

Transit projects that can achieve these goals include improved connections between the
various public transportation modes, such as a mobility hub, enhanced bus stop
amenities, and continued implementation of widened sidewalks and additional street
 trees. Pedestrian improvements focus on intersection safety enhancements, including
upgraded curb ramps, tightened radii, and increased visibility. Proposed bicycle
improvements carry over those already identified in previous plans and propose new
projects that enhance connectivity and close gaps. Vehicular circulation projects include
flex streets, future bridge alignments, and curbside management.

Parking (Chapter 7)
The parking chapter is grounded in the parking principles adopted by City Council in 2019,
and the future parking strategies are an extension of those principles. Overall, the goal
will be to manage existing parking supply while focusing on planning for changing parking
needs as future development occurs. Key strategies include encouragement of the “park
once” model for Downtown visitors, enabling short-term curb parking, allocating curb
space for various modes, and expanding the Transportation Demand Management
program.

ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT
The Specific Plan is subject to CEQA, and to satisfy CEQA requirements, the City is
preparing a Program Environmental Impact Report (Program EIR). This includes analysis
of Transportation and circulation impacts. The Transportation analysis will assess the
impact of the plan on the area’s Vehicle Miles Traveled and propose relevant mitigations
for any impacts. While not assessed under CEQA, the City is also conducting an
operational analysis of the plan area to determine the potential traffic and circulation
impacts that would result from the plan’s implementation. Since the City is concurrently
preparing the Downtown TOD, Golden State, and Media District Specific Plans, each
study also includes cumulative analysis of all three planning efforts.

NEXT STEPS
Staff conducted a study session with City Council on June 30, 2026, at which point the
draft Specific Plan was made available for public review. Members of the community have
already begun providing feedback to the draft plan, and Staff will incorporate this
feedback into a final plan. Staff will host two additional community open houses on August
30, 2026, and September 2, 2026. Furthermore, Staff anticipates releasing the Draft
Program EIR for public review in Fall 2026.

CONCLUSION
The Downtown TOD Specific Plan provides a comprehensive framework to guide future
growth, housing production, mobility improvements, public investment, and neighborhood
preservation in Downtown Burbank. The plan is intended to help the City comply with
evolving state housing requirements while maintaining a clear local vision for
development. Staff is seeking Transportation Commission feedback to ensure it aligns
 with community priorities and objectives. Additional public outreach, environmental
review, and plan refinement will continue throughout 2026 before the plan is presented to
the Planning Commission and City Council for consideration in Winter 2027.

  DEVELOPMENT

DATE:  August 26, 2026

TO:  Transportation Commission

FROM:  David Kriske, Assistant Community Development Director, Transportation
  BY: Marcos Fuentes, Senior Transportation Planner

SUBJECT: Discussion of the Olive Avenue Bridge Replacement Project and Feasibility
  Study

RECOMMENDATION
Receive an overview of the Olive Avenue Bridge Replacement Project Feasibility Study,
which was recently completed to assess options for rehabilitating or replacing the Olive
Avenue bridge in Downtown Burbank.

BACKGROUND
The Olive Avenue Bridge was completed in 1959 and serves as a vital arterial connecting
Downtown Burbank with the rest of the City. Extending over 1,400 feet from First Street,
the structure spans the I-5 Golden State Freeway, Front Street, the Downtown Burbank
Metrolink Station, active Metrolink and Union Pacific railroad tracks, and the Burbank
Western Channel, connecting to Lake Street at its western terminus. The bridge currently
carries two vehicle lanes in each direction but suffers from substandard sidewalk widths,
low safety railings, stairwells, and aging access ramps. Composed of 10 separate spans,
the structure is part of the State Highway System (SHS) and is co-owned by the City and
Caltrans, making Caltrans a key stakeholder for all capital activities.

Beyond carrying local traffic, the bridge functions as a critical regional gateway, linking
commuters and residents between the Downtown Metrolink Station and the residential
and commercial land uses in Downtown Burbank that contribute to Burbank’s status as a
major regional center. This significance is set to grow with Metro’s upcoming North
Hollywood to Pasadena Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) project, which will run along Olive
 Avenue with planned stops at Lake Street. Its significance is further expanded with the
implementation of Burbank’s long-term land use goals to expand housing and commercial
uses in Downtown Burbank as part of the upcoming Downtown Burbank Transit Oriented
Development (TOD) Specific Plan. Recognizing these expanding multimodal demands,
and in alignment with the City Council’s 2025–2026 Priority Action Plan and Capital
Improvement Program, the City initiated a comprehensive Feasibility Study in March 2025
to evaluate the facility's long-term mobility, structural, and utility needs.

Completed in March 2026, the Feasibility Study confirmed that the 67-year-old bridge is
functionally obsolete, seismically deficient, and suffering from ongoing structural
deterioration. While the study evaluated four distinct concepts (two rehabilitation options
and two full replacement options), it strongly recommended full bridge replacement as the
preferred path forward. Although rehabilitation carries a lower initial construction cost, a
new structure provides a vastly superior 100-year life-cycle cost ($450M–$600M for
replacement vs. $1.4B–$2B for rehabilitation), resolves critical vertical and horizontal
clearance issues for Metrolink and future California High-Speed Rail (HSR), and fully
accommodates street-level bike lanes, expanded sidewalks, ADA-compliant elevators,
and top-of-bridge transit cutouts for transit integration, including the BRT.

To transition from feasibility planning into formal project development, the City has
secured $6.25 million in preliminary phase funding, consisting of $3.9 million in local
Measure R funds, a $2.1 million Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG)
from the STBG/CMAQ grant, and a $250,000 federal earmark. These funds will support
immediate project initiation, including executing a cooperative agreement with Caltrans,
drafting the required Caltrans Project Initiation Document (PID), conducting initial
environmental analyses, and launching community outreach to select a final replacement
alternative.

DISCUSSION

Olive Avenue Bridge Avenue Bridge Feasibility Study (2026)

Launched in March 2025 and completed in March 2026, the Olive Avenue Bridge
Feasibility Study was conducted to update a 2016 study that assessed potential
rehabilitation alternatives for both the Olive and Magnolia Bridges. That earlier study
concluded that the Olive Avenue Bridge was functionally obsolete and recommended
strengthening and widening the structure to accommodate vehicle demand while adding
street-level bike lanes and wider sidewalks. While the City is currently leading a separate,
short-term project to modernize railings along both sides of the Olive Bridge, the 2026
study evaluated the overall facility's existing structural conditions, outlined long-term
 mobility needs, and established actionable project alternatives for future design and grant
funding. Through a series of technical evaluations, the 2026 study analyzed the bridge’s
geometric layout against current Caltrans, Metrolink, and HSR standards. It also
performed structural and seismic performance assessments of major components,
evaluated existing and future utility needs, mapped right-of-way ownerships, and
conducted modeling of present and future traffic conditions and operations through the
corridor. These evaluations confirmed that the aging bridge remains functionally obsolete,
is structurally deteriorating, and exhibits ongoing deficiencies across structural, seismic,
maintenance, utility, and multimodal mobility accommodations.

Due to multi-jurisdiction overlaps, development of the study involved interagency
coordination with key regional stakeholders, including Caltrans, Metrolink, LA Metro, the
Los Angeles County Department of Public Works, and the HSR Authority. Input from
these agencies established clear checkpoints for engagement throughout subsequent
project phases. To future-proof the facility, the study integrated priorities from existing
City planning documents into a unified multimodal design concept, such as the City’s
Complete Our Streets Plan and the upcoming Downtown TOD Specific Plan. These
priorities include wider sidewalks, higher protective railings, elevated Class I or Class IV
bike facilities, enhanced pedestrian lighting and shade, and improved ADA-compliant
vertical accessibility between the bridge deck and ground level. Additionally, the design
incorporates a top-of-bridge transit transfer facility to provide direct connections between
the BRT, local bus routes, and the Downtown Burbank Metrolink Station below. These
priorities served as the basis for a consolidated layout and cross-section that served as
the basis for the concept alternatives presented in the study.

Olive Avenue Bridge Avenue Bridge Feasibility Study (2026) Alternative Comparison

Using the consolidated layout and cross-section, the study developed four project
alternatives evaluating constructability, deliver of mobility priorities, capital cost adjusted
for inflation, and total 100-year life-cycle cost, which accounts for ongoing routine and
major capital maintenance. The first two options focus on rehabilitating the existing
structure through varying degrees of foundation strengthening and deck replacement and
widening. Alternative 1 primarily consists of strengthening columns for seismic retrofitting
and widening the existing deck to achieve the desired cross-section. It would require
approximately $40 million in initial construction cost but assumes a total life-cycle cost of
$2.0 billion. Alternative 2 would also involve seismic retrofitting supporting structures but
would completely replace the top deck. It would cost approximately $80 million to
construct with a $1.4 billion life-cycle cost. While rehabilitation presents lower upfront
capital cost, both options limit the bridge’s expected service life to 75 years, require more
 frequent routine maintenance and retrofits, present uncertainties regarding vertical
clearance for Metrolink and HSR, and offer lower seismic resiliency.

Alternatives 3 and 4 evaluate complete bridge replacement, requiring the demolition of
the existing structure and the construction of a modern facility. Both alternatives also
assume using the same layout and cross-section as Alternatives 1 and 2. However
Alternative 3 has an estimated construction cost of $110 million and a total life-cycle cost
of $600 million. Alternative 4, branded as the "Signature Option," incorporates distinctive
architectural features that not only create an iconic landmark but also would make the
bridge more structurally robust, resulting in the highest estimated construction cost at
$140 million but a lower total life-cycle cost of $450 million due to long-term durability.
Both replacement options yield a 75- to 100-year service life, address all structural and
clearance deficiencies, and achieve significantly lower long-term maintenance costs.
Consequently, the study strongly recommends Alternatives 3 and 4 as the preferred
options.

Funding

Realizing this project will require significant capital funds from internal, but mostly external
sources. The City’s funding strategy consists of $3.9 million in Measure R funds allocated
by the City Council and programmed by the Metro Board in 2025. These funds are
important as they serve as the City’s local matching funds to apply for other state and
federal grants. Additionally, in 2025, the City received a $2.1 million Surface
Transportation Block Grant/Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality grant awarded through
SCAG, and a $250,000 federal earmark secured through the support of Representative
Laura Friedman. These initial funds will support early project development, including
drafting a Caltrans Project Initiation Document (PID), conducting preliminary
environmental analyses, refining architectural concepts, and advancing community
engagement. Staff will actively pursue additional grant opportunities across local, state,
and federal levels to secure full design and construction funding.

ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT
Given the scope, scale, and funding, this project is expected to be subject to the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).
Environmental analysis work will be conducted at future phases of the project, including
as part of completing the Caltrans-required PID and formal approval by the City Council
would be required of any environmental documentation at the Project Approval and
Environmental Documentation (PAED) stage.
 NEXT STEPS
Immediate next steps include initiating community outreach to present study findings and
seeking City Council direction to select a preferred replacement alternative. Concurrently,
staff is executing a cooperative agreement with Caltrans to obligate the $2.1 million
STBG/CMAQ grant and the $250,000 federal earmark, procure consulting engineering
services, and initiate the PID. As a co-owned facility on the State Highway System,
Caltrans approval of this document is required to formally define project scope, finalize
environmental requirements, refine cost estimates, and advance the project into
environmental clearance, which is estimated for completion within four years.
Construction timeline will depend on securing future funding and grant awards, right-of-
way verification, and permitting.

CONCLUSION
The Olive Avenue Bridge represents a strategic local and regional mobility asset for the
City. Despite its critical location over the Downtown Burbank Metrolink Station, its car-
centric design presents a barrier to pedestrians, bicyclists, and transit riders alike. The
2026 Olive Avenue Bridge Feasibility Study, completed in March 2026, concluded that
the bridge is functionally obsolete and delivered four potential alternatives that consider
rehabilitating or replacing the facility to better serve the City’s long-term mobility goals
and needs. Completing the feasibility study and advancing the project is in line with the
City Council’s 2025 - 2026 Priority Action Plan. Additionally, the City has secured $6.25
million in funding for this project. Staff plans to conduct initial project outreach on the
study’s findings and then ask the City Council to continue advancing the project and
pursue additional funding opportunities.
